lines: It's a normal evening. You're cleaning out your grandpa's dusty attic, when you find something strange.
An old hourglass. And the sand inside... is glowing.
You flip it over. Just to see what happens.
Bad idea.
When you open your eyes, the air smells of smoke, fresh bread, and something you'd rather not think about.
You're lying in the middle of a street. Strangers in tunics are staring down at you.
Someone shouts at you in a language you almost recognize. Latin.
Congratulations. You've just arrived in Ancient Rome. The year is one hundred AD.
And you have no idea how to get home.
Rome is the biggest city in the world. Around a million people are packed inside its walls.
Most of them don't live in villas. They live in insulae: apartment blocks up to six or seven floors high.
The higher you live, the cheaper the rent. No elevator, no running water, and if there's a fire... good luck getting down.
And watch your head. Some people simply empty their chamber pots out of the window.
It happened often enough that Roman law dealt with it. If something fell on you from a window, you could sue the people who lived there.
Oh, and during the day, most carts are banned from the streets. So deliveries happen at night.
Which means Rome never really sleeps. It just gets louder.
First problem: you're hungry. Second problem: you have no money.
Romans pay with coins. Bronze asses, brass sestertii, and silver denarii.
Luckily, you spot something shiny in the dirt. One sestertius. Enough for a cheap meal.
You find a thermopolium, a Roman street food bar, with big clay pots built right into the counter.
On the menu: lentils, bread, cheese, and olives.
And on almost everything: garum. A sauce made from fermented fish guts.
Romans loved it the way we love ketchup.
You try it. It's... salty. Very, very salty.
With a full stomach, you wander into the Forum, the beating heart of the city.
Here you'll find temples, law courts, and the Senate house, where the most powerful men in Rome make decisions.
Lawyers argue their cases in the open air, and crowds gather just to watch. It's basically ancient reality TV.
And the walls? Covered in graffiti. Election slogans, jokes, love notes, and insults.
One wall in Pompeii says: I'm amazed, O wall, that you haven't collapsed under the weight of so much boring writing.
Some things never change.
Everywhere you look, there are temples. Romans worship many gods: Jupiter, Juno, Mars, Venus, and dozens more.
Before big decisions, priests might examine the insides of a sacrificed animal, looking for signs from the gods.
Even at home, families keep a small shrine for their household spirits, the lares.
You quickly learn: in Rome, it's better not to anger anyone. Especially the gods.
After a day in Rome, you're covered in dust. Time for the baths.
Public baths are cheap, sometimes even free, and almost everyone goes.
First, the warm room. Then the hot room, heated by fires under the floor. And finally, a cold plunge pool.
There's no soap. Instead, you rub olive oil onto your skin, and scrape it off with a curved metal tool called a strigil.
The baths aren't just for washing. People exercise, play games, gossip, and even do business here.
Now, about the toilets.
Public latrines are long stone benches with holes. No walls, no doors. You sit right next to strangers.
And instead of toilet paper, some people used a sponge on a stick. Probably a shared one.
Maybe... you'll just wait.
The next morning, the whole city is buzzing. There are games at the amphitheater.
The Colosseum can hold around fifty thousand people. And entry is free.
You sit according to your rank. Senators get the best seats near the arena. You get the very top rows.
In the morning, there are animal hunts. Around noon, executions. And in the afternoon, the main event: the gladiators.
Despite what the movies show, gladiators didn't always fight to the death. They were expensive to train, and their owners wanted them back.
The crowd screams, cheers, and argues. It's louder than any stadium you've ever been to.
But if you really want to see Romans go crazy, go to the Circus Maximus.
It's a giant racetrack for chariots, and it can fit around a hundred and fifty thousand people.
Four teams race: the Reds, the Whites, the Blues, and the Greens.
Fans are obsessed. They bet money, they curse rival teams, and sometimes they even fight in the streets.
The chariots fly around the sharp turns. Crashes are common, and very dangerous.
And the best charioteers? Some of them became richer than senators.
Of course, Rome isn't all fun and games.
Fires break out all the time. That's why the city has the vigiles, a force of firefighters and night watchmen.
Badly built apartment blocks sometimes simply collapse.
And at night, the streets are pitch dark. No street lights. If you go out without a torch or a friend, you might not come back with your wallet.
Doctors exist, but there are no antibiotics. Even a small cut could become very serious.
After a few days, you start to fit in. You know a few words of Latin, you know where to find the best garum, and you even have a favorite chariot team.
But one night, you notice something glowing in your bag.
The hourglass. The sand is moving again.
You could stay. Join the legion, see the whole empire, and survive twenty five years of marching.
Or you could go home. To hot showers, toilet paper, and pizza.
You flip the hourglass.
So, would you stay in Ancient Rome, or go back home? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe, because the hourglass isn't done with you yet.
